Am I required to carry it?

Only if your home is in a high-risk zone (A or V) and your mortgage is from a federally regulated lender, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Check your zone on FEMA's flood map.

53.6% of Suffolk County's NFIP policies are in high-risk zones (not 53.6% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Buy it now: most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there's no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). NFIP covers up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents, which is a separate policy. To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. Past aid paid here is in “Did the government pay homeowners after floods?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

Many bills here can keep rising: 58.7% of policies pay less than FEMA's full-risk price. Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. Median premium $983, full-risk $2,174 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$983
  • Median full-risk premium$2,174
  • Pay below full-risk58.7% of 15,344

Years to the full-risk price: By law most premiums cannot rise more than 18% a year (FloodSmart puts it at 18–25% for most policyholders); the cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. At the 18% cap, a policy at today's median premium ($983) would take at least about 5 annual renewals to reach the median full-risk premium ($2,174). This is the limit on how fast a bill can climb, not a forecast of any one policy.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Can I pay less than the sticker price?

Not through a community discount: none of Suffolk County's 43 NFIP communities has one.

No CRS discount (43): Mastic Beach; Amityville; Babylon; Babylon; East Hampton; East Hampton; Huntington; Lindenhurst; Lloyd Harbor; North Haven; Northport; Patchogue; Port Jefferson; Riverhead; Quogue; Sag Harbor; Shelter Island; Smithtown; Southold; Greenport; Bellport; Brightwaters; Sagaponack; Shoreham; Nissequogue; Head Of The Harbor; Poquott; Dering Harbor; Belle Terre; Huntington Bay; Old Field; The Branch; Islandia; Lake Grove; West Hampton Dunes; Asharoken; Brookhaven; Islip; Ocean Beach; Saltaire; Southampton; Southampton; Westhampton Beach.

The Community Rating System cuts NFIP premiums for every eligible policy in a community that does extra flood work. The discount shown is the community's rate; what share of its policies currently receive it is not in this data. Confirm with your agent.

How much flood risk is here?

Relatively High for rivers and heavy rain and Very High for coastal flooding, by FEMA's county rating. That compares this county with others; it is not a forecast for your address.

  • Coastal flood riskVery High
  • Inland flood riskRelatively High

This is FEMA's plain risk rating for the county, a comparison — not a prediction for your home. The rating multiplies expected flood loss by a community factor for social vulnerability and resilience; the percentile below is expected loss alone, so the two can differ. Coastal: expected annual flood loss above about 85% of U.S. counties; FEMA models roughly $25,320,023 of flood loss a year across all its buildings. Inland: expected annual flood loss above about 10% of U.S. counties; FEMA models roughly $193,341,419 of flood loss a year across all its buildings. Any loss figure is a whole-county estimate across all buildings, never one home's expected loss or premium.

Source: FEMA — National Risk Index (flood). Data effective NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 22, 2026.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 33,936 NFIP flood claims and $1.1 billion in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2012, 2011 and 1992.

Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2012 ($850,292,328), 2011 ($46,651,863), 1992 ($45,437,103). Total paid $1,097,872,558: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 33,936 claims since 1978 against 29,237 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

How often do the same homes flood here?

Some homes here flood again and again: 1,118 flood-damage applications in FEMA's disaster-aid records came from homes that flooded more than once.

  • Repeat-flood damage records1,118

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so this counts damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid applications since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Repetitive-Loss Flood Properties. Data effective October 24, 2026; retrieved October 24, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Did the government pay homeowners after floods?

Yes, but not much per household: FEMA approved $78.0 million for homeowners here, about $2,908 per registration, against an average paid flood claim of $40,756.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance.

Reconciliation & data completeness

Our counts are checked against FEMA's official figure and the API's own totals.

In-force count: 29,237 policy units (from 27,969 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). FEMA official reconciliation count pending for this county. Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 27969/27969 fetched; claims: 33936/33936 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why any one premium changes — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
